title: The Problem of Induction and Empiricism
text:
Empiricism posits that all knowledge originates primarily from sensory experience. Major proponents, such as John Locke and David Hume, argued that the mind begins as a 'tabula rasa,' suggesting that reason alone cannot provide substantive knowledge without external input. This school of thought heavily emphasizes observation and scientific method as the ultimate arbiters of truth.

The problem arises particularly with induction. Induction is the practice of assuming that future events will resemble past observations, a concept critical for science but logically problematic. David Hume famously highlighted this flaw by noting that no amount of past successful predictions can logically guarantee the success of future ones. Consequently, many epistemologists treat causality not as a necessary logical truth, but merely as a deeply ingrained expectation derived from repeated experience.
